Is elevated immune monitoring early after cardiac transplantation associated with increased plaque progression by intravascular ultrasound?

Please research this question using your tools. You MUST conclude your final response with exactly one of the following lines: 'FINAL DECISION: YES', 'FINAL DECISION: NO', or 'FINAL DECISION: MAYBE'.

Plan:
1. [ ] Search biomedical literature for evidence linking early post-transplant immune monitoring to IVUS-measured plaque progression.
2. [ ] Assess study findings and whether the association is positive, null, or uncertain.
3. [ ] Record concise evidence in the knowledge graph, then provide a sourced conclusion.

Tool call: go_search_agent
Tool call input: {'knowledge_bases': ['pubmed_papers'], 'search_rounds_budget': 3, 'search_target': 'Determine whether elevated early immune monitoring after cardiac/heart transplantation is associated with increased coronary plaque progression measured by serial intravascular ultrasound (IVUS). Focus on immune monitoring markers such as rejection, immune activation, donor-specific antibodies, or gene-expression/immune surveillance in early post-transplant period, and report study design, timing, IVUS progression outcome, direction and quantitative results.'}

Yes. The most directly relevant evidence is a 2015 observational study of 50 heart-transplant recipients (PMID 25429902). Immune monitoring—an ATP-release assay—was measured at a mean of 63.7 ± 16.4 days after transplant. Investigators compared the results with blinded serial IVUS measurements of matched coronary segments at baseline and one year.

Higher early immune-monitoring scores were associated with greater progression in maximal intimal area (p=0.005), average percent stenosis (p<0.001), plaque volume (p=0.005), and maximal intimal thickness (p=0.001). With a study-derived threshold of 406 ng ATP/mL, rapid maximal intimal thickness progression (≥0.5 mm) occurred in 10/12 patients above the threshold (83.3%), versus 5/38 below it (13.2%); the reported risk ratio was 11.7 (p<0.001), with 66.7% sensitivity and 94.3% specificity.

Thus, elevated early immune monitoring was associated with increased IVUS-measured plaque progression in this cohort. The evidence is observational and does not establish causation. The results retrieved here do not establish comparable IVUS evidence for donor-specific antibodies, rejection episodes, or gene-expression surveillance.

Confirm publication details, design, principal p-values and 406 ng ATP/mL cutoff / rapid intimal thickness progression results.'}

Verified from the PubMed abstract for PMID 25429902: the study, published in *Clinical Transplantation* in 2015, assessed 50 heart-transplant recipients using blinded, matched baseline and 1-year IVUS measurements. Immune-monitoring ATP assays were performed about 64 days after transplant.

Progression across immune-monitoring quartiles was significant for maximal intimal area (p=0.005), average percent stenosis (p<0.001), plaque volume (p=0.005), and maximal intimal thickness (p=0.001). The reported cutoff was 406 ng ATP/mL, with 66.7% sensitivity and 94.3% specificity for rapid maximal intimal thickness (MIT) progression of at least 0.5 mm. Rapid progression occurred in 5/38 patients (13.2%) in the lower-IM group versus 10/12 (83.3%) in the elevated-IM group (p<0.001); the reported risk ratio was 11.7 (p<0.001).

These details are supported by the abstract; full text was not available through the retrieval tool.

Yes. In a single-center observational study of 50 heart-transplant recipients, higher immune-monitoring ATP assay results measured about 64 days after transplant were associated with greater plaque progression on serial IVUS over one year. Progression was significant for maximal intimal area, percent stenosis, plaque volume, and maximal intimal thickness (PMID:25429902; search evidence: `call_HGHCpB0AQigDehWjzd3Kplwb`).

At the study-derived cutoff of 406 ng ATP/mL, rapid maximal intimal thickness progression (≥0.5 mm) occurred in 10/12 recipients above the cutoff versus 5/38 below it; the reported risk ratio was 11.7 (p<0.001). This supports an association, not proof that elevated immune monitoring causes plaque progression. The evidence summarized here is from one observational study and does not establish comparable results for other immune markers.

FINAL DECISION: YES
